items.title: Howard Johnson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2019
items.q: He called me about a couple of weeks later because he’d gotten my number from Mingus... when we did, the last thing he did with the orchestra in Montreux with the Gil Evans arrangements

ctx.x: So you have to know the chord structure and how to get — I’m on this chord and I got to get to the next chord with some kind of movement. Was that something you learned before you played the instrument or did you learn it as you went along? © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

Ooh. Good question. Yeah. It’s hard to say one or the other. The thing is I was always into the bass line, even the Louis Jordan records, the piano players were still playing eight to the bar [scats]. Like that. And I could tell that these root notes meant something to not only the piano players and the bass players, but all the guys who were playing. No one had ever said the word “chord changes” to me, but they were there and there’s no missing them if you were listening. And I always liked arranging. I always…

items.title: 66960_Gil Evans oral history interview
items.q: And let's see, there's Howard Johnson who plays tuba and baritone saxophone. He's the instrumentalist, the ultimate instrumentalist.

ctx.x: For example, the tuba, as large an instrument as it is, it's a very delicate instrument and it needs to be amplified when it's played in a low register, you know. I know when it's played up high and it's shouting you can hear it. But when it's played down low which you can do very beautifully and agilely and all that, it has to have a microphone. It just cannot be heard over the sum total of the decibels that come from that band.

The drum, the guitar the bass and all of that. So I will speak to Howard and ask him if he would consider clipping a little contact mic on that tuba. And it should be able to be solved by having a microphone that he can just use on his own. He can use when he wants to do it and it's going to be loud enough, you know. It can be turned up by somebody who is doing the mixing, but you can't always have those ideal situations. So, those things like that.

Would you at this point name the players and instruments in your band, your present band? And separate them into those who play the accoustical instruments and those who play the electronic ones. Is that too difficult? (LAUGHTER).
